analysis.one_liner: Adds a 7% tax on big corporations' reported book profits to ensure profitable companies pay tax.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 7% tax on the profits that large corporations report on their financial statements (above $100 million), on top of the regular corporate income tax. The point is to tax what companies actually report earning to shareholders and investors, closing the gap between reported profits and taxable income. It includes a credit so companies that already pay full corporate taxes are not taxed twice, and it denies a deduction for the new tax itself. The bill never advanced beyond a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would bear a smaller share of federal revenue when profitable corporations cannot use deductions and credits to reduce their tax bills toward zero. The Treasury would gain a new revenue stream from large corporations, funded by the same companies that report large profits to investors.

how_it_helps.text: It imposes a 7% tax on financial-statement (book) income above $100 million, on top of the regular corporate tax, so profitable corporations cannot pay little or nothing through deductions and credits [S3].
It denies a deduction for the new tax itself, preventing companies from writing it off [S3].
It includes a credit for regular income taxes paid, so the surtax primarily targets corporations whose book profits far exceed their taxable income [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with more than $100 million in annual book income, especially those whose tax bills are far below their reported profits; some of the cost could ultimately be passed to shareholders, workers, or consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations with high book profits

drawbacks.text: Because the tax is layered on top of the regular corporate income tax, some companies would face tax on book income that they already pay tax on under the regular system; the bill offers a partial credit (33% of certain tax liability) but does not fully eliminate overlap [S3].

Taxing financial-statement income is complicated to administer: the bill requires Treasury to write extensive regulations, especially for companies reporting consolidated results across many entities, and accounting disputes would be inevitable [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—forcing corporations whose reported profits far exceed their taxable income to pay a minimum tax on real earnings—outweighs the drawbacks, which are modest: some risk of double taxation at the margin and compliance complexity. The bill was never debated or amended, so design questions were never tested. Its larger failure is procedural: with bipartisan appetite for taxing profitable tax-avoiding corporations evident in that era, a single committee referral was enough to bury it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer introduced the bill on August 6, 2021 [S1].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day—the only action the bill ever received [S5].
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and no vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large profitable corporations, whose reported book profits remain untaxed beyond the regular corporate tax, are better off because the bill died without a vote.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no hearing, markup, or vote—burying it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic support (the sponsor plus one Democratic cosponsor) and died in committee without any vote, so no cross-party positions were ever recorded.

industries.industry: Large profitable corporations (over $100 million in book income)
industries.note: Would owe a 7% surtax on financial-statement profits above $100 million even if they owe little under the regular corporate tax. The bill died, so this cost never materialized.

industries.industry: Corporate tax accounting and advisory services
industries.note: The bill would have created substantial compliance and planning work; because it died, no new demand was created. Included here because the mechanism's complexity is a real feature of the design.

industries.industry: Corporate tax avoidance structures (deductions, credits, shifting)
industries.note: By stalling, the bill left intact the existing system in which large corporations report large book profits while owing little federal tax—a status quo this bill was written to disrupt.
